questions.text: Is the genital ulcer painful or painless, and how many ulcers do you have?
questions.purpose: Painless ulcers suggest primary syphilis (chancre); painful ulcers suggest herpes or chancroid

questions.text: Have you had unprotected sex or sexual contact with a new or unknown partner recently?
questions.purpose: STI risk assessment — determines need for comprehensive STI screen

questions.text: Have you had a fever, generalised rash (particularly on palms and soles), or sore throat alongside the ulcer?
questions.purpose: Secondary syphilis presents with rash on palms/soles, fever, and lymphadenopathy — requires escalation

questions.text: Have you had previous similar episodes of blistering or ulceration in the same area that resolved and recurred?
questions.purpose: Recurrent genital ulceration is characteristic of herpes simplex virus (HSV)

questions.text: Are there any enlarged, tender lymph nodes in your groin alongside the ulcer?
questions.purpose: Inguinal lymphadenopathy with genital ulcer can indicate syphilis, chancroid, or LGV

questions.text: Are you aware of your HIV status, and have you been tested recently?
questions.purpose: HIV co-infection increases severity of STI-related ulcers and alters management
